claims.statement: L2 passage reading comprehension is a multi-component ability associated with decoding/written-word access, vocabulary, grammar and broader language comprehension rather than a single isolated reading subskill.

In meta-analytic L2 reading models, language-comprehension components make a substantial contribution to reading comprehension in addition to decoding, so accurate word reading alone cannot establish text understanding.
Vocabulary knowledge and grammar/construction knowledge show strong relationships with L2 reading comprehension across large research syntheses.

Reading comprehension generally improves as lexical coverage increases, but figures such as 95% and 98% depend on the text, learner, task and comprehension criterion and should not be treated as universal deterministic thresholds.
Level-appropriate easy reading can produce stronger comprehension than text above the learner's estimated level; difficulty itself is not evidence of better learning material.
Extensive reading has positive effects on L2 reading proficiency and related language outcomes across meta-analyses, although intervention designs and populations are heterogeneous.
Recent extensive-reading synthesis suggests that level-attuned text selection and some accountability are associated with stronger effects, while long-term follow-up evidence remains limited.

L2 reading-strategy instruction can improve reading comprehension on average, but effects vary across strategies, pedagogical approaches, learner groups and contexts, and delayed-retention evidence is comparatively sparse in some syntheses.
Reading-while-listening shows only a trivial overall comprehension advantage over reading-only in a broad meta-analysis, with no reliable advantage when the reading-only condition is self-paced.
Success while audio is present cannot by itself establish independent reading because audio can change word access, pacing and segmentation demands.

Repeated reading has evidence for improving reading fluency and can improve comprehension in some L2 contexts, including a Vietnamese EFL study, but performance on a repeatedly exposed passage is not equivalent to transfer to an unseen passage.

In a Vietnamese undergraduate EFL experiment, both unassisted and audio-assisted repeated reading improved reading rate, with larger rate gains under audio-assisted repeated reading; the study does not establish a universal near-A0 comprehension policy.
Reading fluency is broader than raw words per minute and involves efficient, accurate processing that supports comprehension; passage-level fluency is informative but speed alone is not mastery.
Glosses and bounded lookup can support L2 reading and vocabulary learning, but assisted comprehension should remain distinguishable from unaided text comprehension.

A valid early reading progression must test connected-text understanding and later performance on unfamiliar text; sentence-level success, practiced-text speed and support-assisted answers are insufficient evidence of independent connected reading.

The optimal progression from messages to microtexts to graded sustained reading, including exact text length, readiness bands, audio/gloss fading, repeated-reading dose and strategy timing for Vietnamese near-A0 adults, is not established and requires direct product validation.
